newsitem.title: UK: PMI strengthens case for UK fiscal tightening.
newsitem.headline: PMI strengthens case for UK fiscal tightening.

text.p: Evidence that the pound's lengthy rally is hitting demand for British goods abroad is a final reminder to the government that its budget should contain measures to cool consumer demand and take pressure off interest rates and the pound, analysts said.

The purchasing managers' index (PMI) said while manufacturing expanded for the 13th month in succession in June, the pace of growth eased and demand for British goods abroad has been hit by the pound's relentless climb.

"This survey is really a timely reminder that the Chancellor needs to take action to dampen consumer demand and ease the upward pressure on the pound," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown will present his first budget to Parliament on Wednesday.
He is expected to tighten fiscal policy by around four billion pounds, but some economists said this will not be enough to stop the Bank of England raising interest rates again in the summer.
They fear further interest rates will drive the pound even higher and further undermine demand for British exports.
Loynes said the outlook for the manufacturing sector was rather bleak.

"This survey contains strong hints about what might lie ahead for manufacturers if the pound keeps rising. And the forward-looking CBI survey suggests exports are going to weaken further in the summer."
Export orders actually grew in June and picked up pace slightly, but the rate of growth has eased considerably since last summer, the survey showed.

"The continued strength of the pound was reported to again have subdued demand for UK goods overseas," the survey said. "Recent slow growth has been sustained largely by an upturn in the rate of economic growth of some overseas markets."
Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS, agreed the survey provided some last food for thought for the Chancellor as he applies the finishing touches to his budget speech.
"The message from this survey and the CBI survey is that export growth is being affected by the pound and growth in the manufacturing sector is rather anaemic."

But he said since the pound will depress economic activity going forward, it could mitigate against much higher interest rates, providing some measures are taken in the budget to address robust domestic demand.
"Providing there is a bit of fiscal tightening directed at the personal sector on Wednesday, there shouldn't be the need for the Bank to raise rates that aggressively," Cates said.
Most economists agree some interest rate rises at least are on the cards.

"If spending power is to be removed from the economy it is difficult to believe this can be achieved entirely without some further increase in interest rates," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
The newly empowered Bank of England's monetary policy committee meets a week after the budget and will deliver its decision on interest rates on July 10.
Financial markets have factored in a half point rate rise before the end of the third quarter with a further quarter point rise by the end of the year.
